title: Ashvala and the fire within
hookLine: the king's own priest asks how a ritual can free anyone from death, and Yajnavalkya shows him the fire is inside him too
tomorrow: when a person dies, what doesn't leave them?

lines: EXPLAIN MY OWN JOB TO ME.
cards: The first challenger is a professional. Ashvala is King Janaka's hotri, the priest whose job at the great fire sacrifice is to recite the hymns of the Rig Veda.
He has spent his life inside the ritual: the right verse, the right moment, the right pitch. So he doesn't ask about the meaning of life. He asks about his own job.
You think you're the wisest? Fine. Explain to me how what I do actually works.

teach.h: CAUGHT BY DEATH: HOW TO GET FREE?
teach.b: Yajnavalkya, Ashvala says, everything here is caught by death. By what does the one who offers the sacrifice get free of death?

teach.h: THE PRIEST IS SPEECH; SPEECH IS FIRE.
teach.b: By the hotri priest, Yajnavalkya answers, by fire, by speech. Speech is the hotri of the sacrifice. Speech is this fire.
That is freedom; that is freedom beyond. Ashvala presses: caught by day and night? By the priest who handles the offerings, by the eye, by the sun.
By the waxing and waning moon? By the priest who sings, by breath, by wind. And the sky has no stairs.
How does the sacrificer climb to heaven? By the priest who oversees, by the mind, by the moon. See the pattern.

teach.h: FOUR PRIESTS, FOUR FACULTIES, FOUR POWERS.
teach.b: Each of the four priests turns out to be a part of the person, speech, eye, breath, mind, and each of those a power of the cosmos, fire, sun, wind, moon. Yajnavalkya doesn't tell Ashvala the ritual is useless.
He shows him what it's a picture of. Ashvala's technical questions get answers too, and he falls silent.
Many teachers see this as one of the great moves of the Upanishads: the yajna, the fire offering, carried inward. Hindu thinkers weigh it differently.
The Mimamsa school held that the rites themselves are the heart of the Veda; Vedanta teachers read passages like this as the rites pointing past themselves.

teach.h: THE FIRE IS IN YOU TOO.
teach.b: Both kept the fire. So when a family pours ghee into a havan fire today, on this reading the offering happens in two places at once: in the flames, and in the people saying the words.

how: Vedic fire rituals, with their four kinds of priests, are still performed in parts of India, and many Hindu homes keep a smaller fire offering, the havan or homa, for occasions like housewarmings and weddings; Vedanta teachers read passages like this as showing the inner meaning of the rite.

s: Ashvala's first question is how the sacrificer gets free of death
everything is caught by death; by what does one get free?
the Upanishads threw out the old fire rituals
Yajnavalkya shows what each part of the rite pictures, and fire offerings are still made today.
after his technical questions are answered, he falls silent.

games.q: at a havan, a friend whispers: 'so this is just pouring butter into a fire?' by Yajnavalkya's answer to Ashvala, what fits?
o: the fire is speech, and each priest is a part of you: the rite pictures an offering of yourself.
it's an old custom; nobody really knows what it means anymore.
it's a trade: you feed the gods ghee, and they send you good luck back.
games.why: Yajnavalkya maps the priests to speech, eye, breath and mind. the outer fire is real, and it pictures an inner offering.

practice: If your home has a diya or a puja shelf, light the lamp, or just picture one; any light will do. Offer it your speech first, the words forming in your mind, like ghee into a flame.
Then let your resting eyes be the sun, the breath coming and going the wind, and the mind watching all of it the moon. Nothing to perform: you're the whole offering, sitting still.

wordCard.voice: Atimukti, freedom beyond. Ashvala's answer: the freedom the rite points to, when the priest is understood as speech, and speech as fire.

orig.note: Sanskrit ati (beyond) + mukti (freedom): "that is freedom, that is freedom beyond."

carryVoice: Hold on to this: the fire rite points within. Tomorrow, a question about what stays when we die. See you then.
